utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, good morning everyone. This is the first occasion on which we are sitting for either a morning or afternoon session, and if I might simply indicate that normally we will sit for two periods of an hour and a half and one of roughly an hour to finish. And these will be interrupted by breaks which will only be 20 minutes or so, so they're going to be difficult to deal with. But the object of the exercise is obviously to sit for a minimum of four hours, if we can, each day. Now, Mr. Stamp, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. He is present in court. He is Nike Peraj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Peraj, would you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Says the witness in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please be seated. Now, Mr. Peraj, what language will you generally use in the course of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My mother tongue; Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you please state your name.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Nike Peraj.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I understand, Mr. Peraj, that until June 1999 you were a member of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when you left the army, what rank were you?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Captain of the first order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And under what -- when, precisely, and under what circumstances did you leave the army?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Three days before the Yugoslav army withdrew from Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I went to my home, and -- and didn't go any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And where was your home at that time?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: The building near the high school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, if I'm not mistaken, what you wanted to establish was why the witness left the army, or have I misunderstood your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Not exactly, but that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the question was under what circumstances did he leave the army. Is that not why did he leave the army?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Quite similar to why. Circumstances may not necessarily incorporate the motive, but I could lead him because it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, are you not intending to pursue that? Because you're not getting an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I will pursue it because I think it should come from his mouth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You are -- you deserted the Army of Yugoslavia when you departed?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: In fact, I didn't desert the army. I just stayed in my hometown, in my place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you subsequently receive any information as to any proceedings or action that the army took in respect to your remaining at home?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Officially not. I wasn't notified of any such proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Did you hear from anyone as to whether or not there were any proceedings?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I heard from a friend of mine that because of that reason, I was taken to the military tribunal without me being present and sentenced to 15 years of prison. This was proven to me also in this very tribunal by the deceased Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, did you give various statements to investigators of the OTP, including a statement in April 2000, February 2001, and on the 8th of May, 2002?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And since you arrived here for testimony in this case, did you review another statement which incorporated what you had said in those previous three statements plus a few additional comments that you wanted to make? And this was on the 9th of August this year.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the matters in that statement that you reviewed on the 9th of August are correct to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That, Your Honours may it please, is Exhibit P2253.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, unlike some of the other documents you presented with witnesses, this one is presented exclusively in terms of Rule 89(F).

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. Thank you. Could we put on the screen Exhibit P325. I don't propose to take a long time because the statement is quite long and comprehensive, but I think I could try to make sense out of a couple of maps that he referred to in his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the course of giving a statement, the second statement, in 2001, did you mark on a map the positions where various units of the Yugoslav military forces were and where the population movements were on the 27th and the 28th of February, 1999?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we have on the screen Exhibit P325, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sir, can you make out that map on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is that the map on which you marked certain places and positions that you were showing to the investigator during your statement?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, could we have a look at Exhibit P326.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And while it is brought up, did you -- were you shown and did you review a computer-generated map which more clearly showed the same markings you had made in the previous map you had seen? And is that the computer-generated map before you?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I just realised that this map on the -- in e-court is in black and white, which it is not supposed to be. The purpose of the computer-generated map was to more clearly show what he had marked, and this doesn't help us. I'm wondering if we could put --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Put it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- a colour copy on the ELMO. May I just make an inquiry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm afraid that map is on A3, and it's probably a little bit too large for the ELMO. Could you put it -- put the map further up so we could see the lower part of the map on the screen. Okay. Right there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you gave a lot of details in your various statements about the events of the 27th and the 28th of April [Realtime transcript read in error "February"] in which you personally witnessed the --

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understood your earlier questions to be related to the 27th and 28th of February, but that's a mistake, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Again, the transcript is showing February. What month is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's April 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There are some green lines to the southern or to the bottom part of the map, green broken lines. Can you make out those lines?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. What do they signify?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: They show the positions of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, do you know which unit of the Yugoslav army, or units?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: There were several units of the Gjakova Brigade, of Prizren, and Prizren [as interpreted], which I have seen myself, I have visited before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not sure that that's accurately reflected in the transcript either. Could you clarify, Mr. Peraj, what units of the Yugoslav army were there, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The -- I have indicated that with the arrows running on the side of the green. I have displayed it in green, actually. That was Brigade number 68 -- 63 of the parachutists of Nis. That with blue shows the special units of MUP of Serbia. The broken lines on the side, also in green, show the presence of the garrison of Gjakova and Prizren soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you're saying that they -- or I should ask you. The two green lines with the arrows at the end signify what? What do the arrows in particular signify?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: One is actually blue, one is -- the blue shows the positions of the special forces of Serbian MUP, the direction they assaulted, whereas the green arrow indicates the forces of the Brigade number 63, Parachutist Brigade of Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that green arrow also indicates the direction in which they were moving. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Both arrows show the direction from where they have attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, across the middle of the map there's a broken black line with the numbers indicating dates on two sides of it; one 27/4/99 and the other below saying 28/4/99. What do those dates and the broken black line signify?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: The date of 27th of April, 1999, shows where the attack was interrupted at night and that it continued, it resumed, on the second day, on the 28th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, on which page of the statement do we find matters relating to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is -- may I refer to a paragraph number instead because we are talking about different languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think this is from paragraphs 57 until 97.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the broken black line across the middle, what does that indicate? Do you see that on the map?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: The red line, which is in the middle, indicates the direction of the movement of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, as you're speaking about red lines, there are two red lines. Could you just indicate what each one signifies.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: One of them indicates the direction of population movement, which went in the direction of Junik. From Junik, Dobrosh, Sheremet, Dallashaj, Racaj, Meja, Gjakova.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that --

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Whereas the second line signifies the movement which goes from Korenica, Orize, in the direction of Gjakova.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The second line is the one going across the page, at the bottom of the page, going from left to right across the bottom of the bottom. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Which one, which of the red lines you refer to as the second line, signifying the movement of people from Korenica to Djakovica city?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: On my left. That is the one that shows this --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was asking if that is the one that is going from left to right at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Peraj, where the lines meet each other, what happened there? We seem to have two -- the map represents two convoys of refugees. Did they cross over each other or did they sort of merge together and go in two directions at that point? Can you clarify that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the crossroads at Orize, where both convoys met. But after that, some people in one convoy went in the direction of Albania from Qafa e Prushit. The remainder continued their voyage towards Gjakova, Prizren, reached Morine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, back to the broken black lines across the middle of the map between the two dates. What do those lines signify?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've had an answer to that, Mr. Stamp, to say that was the point they reached on the 27th, overnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do they signify anything apart from that, Mr. Peraj?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: This shows that at night they stopped and then they continued the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. Very well. Now, you have indicated with red circles two check-points.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in your statement you refer to a check-point that was in front of the store of Krist Sokoli, just opposite the school where you saw four dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Paragraph number?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is paragraph 69, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall that, Mr. Peraj?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Which check-point is that on the map in front of you? Or to your left, actually.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: It's the crossroads where both arrows, both lines, cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You also spoke of another check-point in front of somebody by the name of Hasanaj's house. Do you recall speaking about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For the record, that's paragraph 73 and thereafter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that, I take it, would be the other check-point indicated on the map?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: In fact, that shows the movement of the population. That was the first place where the population met in Meja.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. And that is the second check-point on the map?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes, according to their direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You also --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, it's not clear to me. But if by "second check-point" you mean the same one, then it's clear, because Meja appears on the map near the one you've already referred to. It's not entirely clear to me that these are simply two isolated check-points, of course. You've haven't established that there only are two, albeit there are circles, but they're very big circles.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that the second part is not at all clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness could be given a pen and could we ask him to mark the check-point on the map, just to make it absolutely clear, since there are very big circles.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is there something you would like to say, Mr. Peraj?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I want to make a clarification. According to the direction of the population towards the south of Carragojs, that convoy of people, that met at the cross-point, the first cross-point, which was in Meja. The second cross-point for the same group of people was Orize, whereas for the people coming from Korenica in the direction of Gjakova, the second cross-point for -- first, excuse me, for them was Orize.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. I'm going to ask you to put -- can you see that map beside you to your left? To your left.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is it possible for you to put a number 1 in the circle at the check-point which you describe as the check-point -- the first check-point for the population moving south from the Carragojs area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, the one -- Mr. Peraj, the one that you've marked number 1 has within it the name Meja Orize, and in your previous answer you said that that was the second check-point for the group of people coming down the valley.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we take -- I've been there myself. If we take, for me, the first point was Orize. The second was Meja. This is how I have seen them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But if we look at the direction of the population towards Llugu i Carragojs --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I ask this by way of clarification --

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: -- for them, Meja was the first check-point. For them, again, the second check-point was Orize.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. I think --

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Whereas for the people that moved from Korenica in the direction of Gjakova, the first check-point was in Orize.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, unless I can't see an Orize -- a second Orize on the map, then the bottom convoy doesn't appear to go through Orize. It may be this is an example of maps simply confusing the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm certainly confused at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's take this step by step. The check-point you have marked number 1, Mr. Peraj, and that is where the two convoys meet, that is a check-point where? What is the area where that check-point is called?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: The check-point I put a number 2 is Orize, check-point near the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. And the one above that, what is that area? What do you call that area?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Where I've put number 1 in Meja was in the vicinity of Hasanaj's home.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we just go back. You marked a check-point on the map. Could you point to it, please. Point to the check-point that you marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He's marked two check-points on the map. He's put a 1 and a 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The check-point that you marked number 1 -- I'm sorry to have to ask you again. The check-point that you marked number 1, what area is that check-point in?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Check-point number 1 is in Meja, near the house of Hasanaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And check-point number 2 is in what area?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Check-point number 2 is in Orize, near the school, and the store of Krist Sokoli, Krist Sokoli.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So just for clarification, you are saying that check-point number 2 would be the first check-point that the population moving from Korenica would pass through. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And check-point number 1 would be the first check-point that people coming down the Carragojs valley would then come to?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But you were coming, according to your statement, from Djakovica when you went to the first check-point. Could you point to the first check-point you went to which you describe in your statement, and that is a check-point in front of the school. Just point it again, please.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So the first check-point you went to is the one marked number 2.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you have marked the MUP command post with a blue circle. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you have marked the VJ command post with a green circle. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said in your statement that both command posts had a clear -- or from both command posts there was a clear view of the valley. I would like to ask you these two questions specifically: In respect to the MUP command post, could the two check-points be seen from that command post?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: No. Only the direction of the police forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could the two check-points be seen from the VJ command post?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we briefly -- thank you very much. Could that be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sabbah, a number for that?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that will be Exhibit IC8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we put on the computer screen, please, Exhibit P328.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, is that a map of all of Djakovica, the shaded area being the area where the operation took place? Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we make it a little clearer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but it doesn't show the entire territory of Gjakova. This shows only the territory where the operation took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that is the shaded area?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes. In this shaded area, the operation took place, whereas the map shows the territory of Gjakova, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Finally, you said that General Lazarevic coordinated the operation from Djakovica. How did you become aware of this?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: The night of the 28th of April -- correction, in the morning of 28th of April I ask, if possible, to go and visit my home in my native village. So I had to ask permission to enter that zone. I was there together with Sergej Perovic. In the basement of a building near Cafe Lajic, that is Lajic Cafe, was General Lazarevic, Lieutenant-Colonel Jeftovic, who followed in the map the operations -- the operation taking place on the ground which continued on the 28th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The building near Cafe Lajic is in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you go into the basement of the building?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you go into any particular room or office of that building?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Whose room or whose office was it?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: That was where Lieutenant-Colonel Jeftovic was. And the general was quite near, General Lazarevic was quite nearby.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, which paragraph is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is paragraph 65. I'm sorry, Your Honour, I tried to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- to make references to the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you said -- I get it from the translators that you said there was General Lazarevic, Lieutenant-Colonel Jeftovic, who followed in the map the operations. What are you speaking of? What map and what operations are you speaking of?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I mean the operation of Llugu i Carragojs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's the operation in the Carragojs valley on the 27th and 28th [Realtime transcript read in error 28th and 29th] of April, 1999. Is that what the map indicated?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes, the 27th and the 28th, not the 29th. It was the 27th and the 28th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. You -- in your statement you refer at various passages --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're moving off that subject?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm moving off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a comment. The -- when I read this paragraph 65, I wrote in the margin: What is the source of this information? And you've obviously clarified that with the question, because when you read the statement it's not at all clear how he knew this information. And yet here we have, I would have thought, the sort of information that really matters in this trial and it's not mentioned in the statement. It's puzzling to me that that's how these statements are compiled. In any event, carry on to the next topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In -- at various parts of your statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And for the benefit of the Court, primarily paragraphs 21, 37, and 51.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- you refer to a Major Nikola Micunovic. Was he a member of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And lastly, because it is not altogether clear from your statement, you said that on that afternoon you left -- the afternoon of the 27th you left the cultural centre and went to the Catholic church to take your family, and you did so with your brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This, Your Honours, is at paragraph 67.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Why did you go to tell your -- to take your family? Did your brother tell you anything?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: He told me -- he arrived and told me that they had been expelled, they had to get out, leave their house, and that in Meja a lot of people had been arrested and detained -- no, they were not arrested, they were stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did your brother live in Meja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he didn't live in Meja. He lived in Dallashaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Now, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I want a little clarification on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry to bother you with a bit of clarification which I'm seeking. You said that you went away to your home. I mean, you were in the army, you went away to your home. And repeatedly when questioned you did not explicitly state the reason for going home. Is it already contained in paragraph 19, 20, 21, and 25 of your written statement? Should we take that as the reason, because you didn't want to say it orally?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before he answers, Your Honour, he doesn't have the statement in front of him. So if he could be given a copy, it might be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I think the -- I'm sorry, I was referring to one of the statements which was given to me, but the one which he has supplied to the Court overall for use would correspondingly have paragraphs 69, 70, et cetera. Does he rely on that for explaining why he -- why he stayed back home?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, he's referring to paragraph 8 in the statement, should I call the compendium statement -- the compilation statement of the 9th of August. Paragraph 8 deals with the issue that Your Honour is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Peraj, could you look at paragraph 8 of your statement in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not the point that's being made, Mr. Stamp. We've already had the information in paragraph 8. What Judge Chowhan is asking is what was the reason for desertion. And he's asking if it's contained in the section which starts about paragraph 69 and thereafter, or is he able to give some other explanation for staying at home and not returning to the army? Can you help us on that, Mr. Peraj? Judge Chowhan is anxious to know, what was your reason for abandoning your duties in the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to say first of all that I didn't take an active part as a member of the Yugoslav army. I did not take part in any action, in any operation. And I had over 20 family members in Dallashaj, 21 family members. And I did not think it reasonable after the -- they withdrew, that I should go back to Serbia with them because otherwise I would have become an enemy of my own people. I would have been known as an enemy of my people, without having done anything wrong to anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Peraj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, we have the order for cross-examination. General Lazarevic, General Pavkovic, General Ojdanic, Mr. Milutinovic, Mr. Sainovic, and General Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Peraj, I am Mihajlo Bakrac, attorney-at-law, member of the Defence team for General Lazarevic. Mr. Peraj, in your statement you said that on the 21st of December, 1998, you took over your duties in the 52nd Artillery Rocket Brigade in Djakovica. And that is paragraph 4 of your latest statement. Can you tell me what your duty was exactly in terms of establishment?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I was the second assistant in the operational staff, teaching staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you tell me -- is it correct that in paragraph 6 of your statement - I'm talking about the statement dated the 8th and 9th of August, 2006 - did you say there that the 52 Artillery Rocket Brigade was directly subordinate to the VJ Corps headquarters in Pristina and that the VJ Corps headquarters received orders from the Ministry of Defence in Belgrade? Is that the chain of command that you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: The 52nd Brigade in Gjakova was under the command of the corps, whereas the corps itself was under the command of the army in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And the army in Nis?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: And the army in Nis was under the command of the General Staff in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you stated what I read out to you just now, what I quoted?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I -- that's what I said and that's, as far as I'm aware, the way it was, but there might be a translation mistake somewhere. I don't know. But that, what I just said, is the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But in your statement you said that the corps command received orders from the Ministry of Defence. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: That's not what I stated. Maybe that is a mistake made by someone else. Maybe somebody wrote it down that way, but that's not what I said. I know that, at least. It was that -- I was telling you who was in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Peraj, in another paragraph of your statement, in paragraph number 10 that is, you said that there was a law that during wartime other structures would come under the command of the VJ. These other structures were the MUP and components of the TO, the Territorial Defence. In paragraph -- or rather, I beg your pardon. I mean: What did you mean when you said that according to the law -- or rather, that that is the way it was according to the law?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I know, according to the constitution, that all armed forces, including the police, Territorial Defence, and all the rest, are all under the command of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So that's what you read in the constitution, right?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Well, that's the way it was, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show Defence Exhibit 5D4. Could we have it on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just to indicate to the Court, these have not been disclosed to us. Neither have we received any notification, as required in the order on procedure and evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's difficult to accept when it's already in e-court, is it not? What's happened here, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did place this on e-court, but perhaps I'm wrong in believing that this was already part of the Prosecution disclosure. This is the law on national defence -- or rather, the law on defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you're saying it's not a Prosecution exhibit but it's a document given to you by the Prosecution in the course of disclosure?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That document was in that set of documents submitted by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm trying to find the document. If it is the law on defence, if it is something that the Prosecution would have disclosed to the Defence, then it would have -- it will be tendered by the Prosecution through a witness eventually, or if the Court so orders in a -- in response to a motion that we have filed for the receipt of evidence, if that is it. But we are trying to find the document that has been referred to, and I think we have. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does -- well, first of all, does it have a P number?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, it does, but it would take some time to find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We could overcome these difficulties if the order of July -- the order of the Trial Chamber of the 11th of July, at paragraph 3, that a list of the documents and other materials to be used by the party when cross-examining a witness be disclosed to the opposing party, then we would have it and we would be able to give the Court all the information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bakrac, that order remains in force. I appreciate that there's been a request to reconsider it, and that's being given active consideration and will be dealt with in the course of this week, but you should, on the basis of the existing arrangements, have disclosed specifically a list of the documents that you would be referring to. Now, why was that not done?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I already explained that I thought that while -- in view of -- well, I thought it was in the Prosecution's set of documents. So from the very outset I actually misunderstood this. Well ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the order requires more than that. It requires you to list the items which you will be using, and indeed the request to reconsider acknowledges that that step should be taken but suggests that a different time-frame should be employed, and the time-frame should be once the witness has taken the solemn declaration. So at this point in time, even on the basis of the request to reconsider, a list should have been given to the Prosecution. Now, they are not taking serious exception to this and therefore we can proceed, but other Defence counsel should note the point that if there are documents to be used in the course of cross-examination of this witness, they should be immediately disclosed in the form of a list to the Prosecution. Carry on, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. In the meantime we found it, if it will be of assistance. This is P1874.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, can I again make a practical suggestion. When we have P1874, unless there is some -- some difference in the more or less identical Defence document, it's simply going to cause confusion and unnecessary work if we bring in an additional exhibit. So it would be helpful not to refer to 5D4, unless there's something peculiar about it you want to rely on. If it's simply a question of a document that there is no dispute over the terms of, then please use, if you can identify it, the Prosecution exhibit number. All right. Thank you. So we'll use P1874.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So this is the law on defence. And in paragraph 17 -- or rather, article 17 it says the following: "In the case of imminent threat of war, a state of war, or a state of emergency, the units and organs of the Ministry of the Interior may be used for carrying out combat tasks." Mr. Peraj, that's what this law says, they may be used. It's not that they have to be used and that there has to be resubordination. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I agree they can be used, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Peraj. Since you have agreed with me on this, in paragraph 46 of this last statement of yours, you said that all armed groups of the Army of Yugoslavia, the MUP, and others were subordinate to the VJ in theory. Is that what you meant, what we agreed on just now; in theory, according to the law, they may be used?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: First of all, I can say that the police forces were used even before. But as to your second question, the situation -- as I said, the situation on the field was completely different at that time. Coordination between the army and other forces was not at the requisite level, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Peraj. Do you know that in the second half of April, orders were written on resubordination that were never actually implemented?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Which paragraph are you talking about? Where did I say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Peraj. That's not what you said. That is my question. Do you know that in the second half of April, towards the end of the month of April, orders were written on resubordination that were never actually implemented? The resubordination of the MUP to the army. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: No, I don't know about written orders like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in paragraph 11 of your statement, you stated that the MUP was subordinated to the VJ commander or leadership, but this happened only on the basis of agreements?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in another paragraph, in paragraph 12 of this statement, you said that paramilitary units were not under the control of the VJ army? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: No, they weren't, because in the barracks, the -- there were normal soldiers and they were not allowed to enter the barracks. There were only reservists of the armed forces, which --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Peraj. I just put this very brief question to you. Is it correct, Mr. Peraj, that in paragraph 15 of your statement you said that the commanders of the Army of Yugoslavia in Djakovica arrested many of the regular soldiers and reservists who committed different types of crimes. Is that correct? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that in the same paragraph you stated that the military court convicted five of them, five out of eight reservists. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I heard about that from officers in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Peraj. Is it correct that also in paragraph 15 you stated that you know that the commanders of the Army of Yugoslavia did not order soldiers to commit crimes and that these were only isolated cases?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Peraj. Is it also correct that you stated that a number of reservists at the beginning of the war joined the paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bakrac, there can, in appropriate circumstances, be good reasons for a cross-examiner going back over exactly what a witness has said in examination-in-chief. There can be reasons for it, but in a court of this nature, where there's no need to be grandstanding to a jury or emphasising points in examination for effect, whether dramatic or otherwise, it's doubtful if there's any useful purpose to be achieved by simply reiterating the favourable points from the statement for your case. That can all be dealt with in your arguments in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I'll try. I thought that I should draw the witness's attention to those parts of his statement that are important for our Defence, for our Defence team, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what's your reason for doing that? I mean, if there's a good reason, then I --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because in the last statement, there -- well, it seems contradictory and unclear as to what is correct and what is not. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, this is all argument, Mr. Bakrac. It would be helpful if you would confine the cross-examination to what's controversial.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Peraj --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, page 26:20 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Paragraph, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, page 26, line 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yeah, of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of the transcript, there is no answer of the witness. It wasn't recorded. The witness said yes. I heard that, but it was not recorded in the transcript. 26, 20. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, you're correct from my -- according to my recollection, Mr. Zecevic. So we can regard the answer at line 23 as relating to the whole of that question. All right. Thank you very much. Carry on, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Peraj, is it correct that at the Milosevic trial you stated that reservists came to military units, but when they saw that they could not take that kind of discipline, then they decided to join the paramilitary forces. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes, there have been many cases like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In your statement, Mr. Peraj, you talk about territorial units. At that time, did the Territorial Defence still function?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I think there were some changes in the names of the forces. Every municipality had its own force. Earlier they were called Territorial Defence. These were forces which were mobilised and were commanded by Nikola Micunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And they were subordinate to who?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: The mayor of the municipality of Gjakova, who during -- in wartime is the main commander of Territorial Defence for the municipality --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the Micunovic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and who is de facto commander, or under the -- under the command of the commander in -- of the barracks, if a barracks exist there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The Micunovic you've now mentioned is a different person from the Micunovic about whom you were asked questions by Mr. Stamp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's the same person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, the same person. I thought the previous one was Dragan Micunovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it is Nikola Micunovic, but we also call him Dragan. He has two names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Peraj, will you agree with me that this Territorial Defence, as you call it, was responsible to the military district, not the corps command?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: It could be that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Peraj. You talked about Nikola Micunovic now and you called him "Dragan." Is it correct that he was an administrative officer in the military department when there was no state of war?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Peraj, in your statement, in paragraph 22 you said that in the area of Djakovica there were over 170 tanks.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. That's what I said, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said that you know that because a man who was at the fuel point had just fueled 60 tanks on that day, on the 27th.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: That's true, but only on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in the transcript -- or rather, in the Milosevic case you said that, as far as this was concerned, that person told you that he had fueled 40 tanks rather than 60 tanks?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: That's possibly a mistake. I said "60" and I have material to prove that there were 60.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Since there may be a dispute on this, can you give us a transcript page number for the Milosevic trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. It is page 4707, lines 6, 7, 8, 9, and 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Peraj, are you telling me now that there was a total of 60 tanks. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that there were 60 in all. There were more tanks in the territory of Gjakova than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I'm so sorry, Your Honour. I have the impression that you wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, no. Once you've completed this point, we can have our break.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But tell me now, on the basis of this fact, that this person told you that he had fueled 60 or 40 tanks, how did you come to the conclusion that there were over 170 of them?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: The person, who we say in Serbian was "tankirao," he told me they went to get fuel. And he said: I'm really tired because all day today I've been busy filling the -- filling up all the tanks with fuel, 60 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll break there and try to resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Peraj, is it correct that you stated that at the end of February and in early March in the area of Djakovica there was a Republika Srpska Brigade there?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: That brigade from the RS was in the area of Djakovica to try and prevent any attacks from Albania and to provide security for those units which were in front of the others?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said that brigade had T-55 tanks. Do you know where those tanks were from?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes, although I'm not sure where they came from. I think -- I think they belonged to them, because if they were to take up other tanks, to bring in other tanks, it would have taken too much time to -- to exercise the tank units, the people running the tanks. So they could have been brought in from Serbia because there were tanks there and other anti-aircraft equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, they were also used for anti-aircraft defence. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Not the tanks themselves but the other equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Peraj, did you know that as of the 10th or 11th of April, 1999, there was a land attack on the national border towards Albania?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but at the time there were sporadic attacks at the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Peraj, you say "sporadic attacks." Did you know that at that time, on the axis of Rosevo and Gorazup, there were 113 [Realtime transcript read in error "a great number"] killed and a great number of soldiers wounded by the KLA attacks carried out at the national border?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I don't know the number. I said "sporadic." What I meant by this was from time to time there were attacks, there were encounters with Serb forces. And where -- at the places on the border where Serb forces were defending.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I thought I heard a specific number in your question, but it's not reflected in the transcript. Was there a specific figure of persons killed or did you just say there were a number killed?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I mentioned a specific number. There were 113 killed and 375 wounded soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And are you posing the question on the basis that that was on a specific date or dates, or over a period of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During April, when that operation of attacking the national border was carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, does that mean your question relates specifically to the 10th and 11th of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Perhaps it's better if I reformulate it, the question. I wanted to ask the witness if he knew that those attacks at the national border lasted throughout April and even in May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I know of sporadic attacks, but not of large or long attacks. And at the end of March or the beginning of April, I don't remember, but I do know there were -- that a lot of military people who died from NATO bombings, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Since you mentioned NATO bombings, did NATO planes often target Djakovica and its surroundings?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: They attacked various localities, in particular the old barracks in Gjakova and the radar in Ljupanar [phoen], and a few other places, mostly where they thought the armed forces were situated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did they also bomb Cabrat, which is not far from the old town in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes. But Cabrat, there were no losses in Cabrat. There was an improvised maquette of tanks there, a model of tanks, a fake model, to lead the planes in on short wave, and there were stoves there for heating to show that there was warmth so that the planes would hone in on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Peraj, are you familiar with the Operation Arrow 1?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I've heard about it, but I didn't read the documents, the specific documents, about it, but I did hear about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Have you read the book entitled "Boj Na Kosarama," "The Battle at Kosara"?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you know that, apart from members of the KLA, some foreign mercenaries also used to cross the national border?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I don't remember. For foreign mercenaries, as you say, yes, there were KLA. They did cross the border, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you know that in Djakovica at the cemetery, some KLA members were buried, but they were not of Albanian background, ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I don't know. For the Albanians, I know that there were Albanians buried there who were members of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Peraj. You will agree, I believe, then, that there were fights in Djakovica between the members of the KLA and the VJ?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: There were no -- there was no fighting in the city of Gjakova.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But there was fighting in the area around the town of Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there was only one case in Cabrat when five or six persons entered the area to visit their families, and they were ambushed by Yugoslav forces. I know in Kosara, Molnice, and up at the border there was fighting, as I said, but they were sporadic, as I said earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were there any attacks on the police and military forces in the Carragojs valley in March and April 1999?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, at the beginning of April there were two cases of which I am aware, in the Llugu i Carragojs. There was one case where Milutin Prascevic was killed with four other policemen, five altogether thus, and two or three days earlier there was another incident where a Montenegrin was killed, Vojislav Pekovic, near the village of Racaj. I know about these two incidents in concrete terms. I know because I took part in the burial of the fellow Pekovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When did those attacks occur, these two attacks? Can you remember the date?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: The exact dates I don't remember because there were a lot of things going on at the time, but I do remember it was in April, April.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Would you agree that it was in the second half of April 1999?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: No. Around the middle of April, not towards the end. Not at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Peraj, would you agree if I said that the forces of the VJ, or some forces of the VJ were grouped along the line of Prizren-Djakovica-Pec?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Would you agree that such deployment of VJ units was a logical choice, given the close proximity to the national border, to Albania, and the length of the border in that area? And you said that in that area there was only sporadic fighting.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I would agree that it would be normal for such forces to be deployed in that area because -- because they were expecting attacks from Albania, that KLA soldiers would be entering from Albania with NATO support. But up to that time - if I may continue - they didn't come -- or at least, there was no confrontation up to that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Peraj, you said yourself it was logical to expect an attack of the KLA which would come alongside other NATO attacks.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I could agree, but it is not logical, however, to expel the whole population of the territory and to massacre the population in Meja. That's not something which should be done. There were entirely civilian population there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Peraj --

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: It is logical, as you say, that forces be deployed in the area because there was a danger coming from the border, but there were no people in the area anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Has the in-depth line starting from the national border up towards the interior of the -- of Kosovo, was it extended from 5 up to 10 kilometres by a decision of the federal government?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I heard that the -- that the border was expanded -- there were three different borders; the first one, the second one, and a third one, a border belt, which means that the whole thing was wider. But they were divided into three sections, one, two, three, and there were major differences in them as to the operations which were carried out in these various belts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you know that in military theory of all modern armies, that in the border belt there should be no civilians in situations such as this one?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that is known, but the situation was entirely different as to what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Peraj --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the witness was about to explain what he meant. Maybe I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it's fairly obvious what he meant. Please carry on, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Peraj, given the fact you just mentioned, that it is a common understanding not to have civilian population in the border belt and that it was logical to expect a land invasion by the joint KLA and NATO forces, wouldn't it also have been logical for the civilian population to leave the area in which such an attack may occur?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: That would be logical, as you say, but to forcefully expel the whole population along the border belt and to expel them to Albania and then to burn all their houses and burn and destroy all their valuables; that's not logical. People were being killed during the expulsions; that's not logical. Why did they burn down their houses?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Peraj, we talked about this Prizren-Djakovica-Pec line just now and this border belt that is closest to Albania. Does it not coincide with what you drew on the map as Exhibit 143 -- or rather, P326? When you talked about the deployment of VJ forces, are those not precisely the lines for which we established that it would be natural to expect them to be attacked from Albania?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: No, no, that's not the lines that I marked. These were lines to support operations undertaken by the police and the 63rd Brigade, but at the check-points there were paramilitary forces and the police, paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Peraj, we've heard about that from your statement. We've heard about that. I'm interested in the following: Is it correct that these lines coincide with what you and I have been concluding now, the border belt, the main roads right next to the border of Albania, which is 57 kilometres long. Do you agree with me? I'm asking you whether those lines coincide.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: The lines show support for the forces. It has nothing to do with the border lines. Those were other forces at the border. And the lines which were drawn there are different, which -- the ones which I drew on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Peraj, it was precisely on this map that you drew this, and today on page 7 of the transcript, lines 18 and 20, you told us that you marked a line where the forces stopped on the 27th and the 28th -- or rather, where they spent the night between the 27th and the 28th. Do you agree that that is far above Meja and Orize?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Look, the forces were not allowed to go further than Meja. At the check-points there were certain forces who were waiting for the people --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: No, sir -- no. Mr. Peraj, P326 is the Prosecution exhibit where you drew a dotted line, and today you explained - and that is on page 7, lines 18 and 20 of today's transcript - you explained that that line is the line where the forces actually stopped on the 27th of April and where they spent the night between the 27th and the 28th of April. Is it correct that this is at the level of the village of Ponosevac, Nec, and Racaj, that are considerably before the village of Meja. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I have to explain something, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 27th the operation began. The forces which were going in the direction of Junik and Dobrosh expelled the population, and the populations went on its way on the 27th. Those who arrived in Meja on that day - because the population was in a state of despair; it was a terrible crisis with arms going off and houses being burnt down - so when they left their houses -- immediately after they left their houses, their houses were burnt down. So they were in panic. And then -- please hear me out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... this is not an answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: They didn't -- they couldn't go around -- they couldn't use side roads. Everything was blocked off. They had to use the main road, the one that I marked on the map. And the forces --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Peraj, hold on. The question you are being asked is seeking clarification of evidence you gave earlier, which is evidence about where the forces that were in the valley spent the night of the 27th of April, and you gave evidence that the broken black line on the map, which is P326, was where they spent the night. And you're being asked to clarify that that is, in fact, the position; and secondly, that that is considerably before the village of Meja. Now, what's the answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Firstly, the line is before Meja, higher; and secondly, the next day the action continued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Peraj, on the 27th of April, the Serb forces were not in the village of Meja. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: No, they were. They were there. At the end -- at the edge of the village of Meja.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say "at the edge," you are talking about a smaller unit that assisted you. In conversation with Scepanovic, I mean. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So this is a smaller unit, and you said that they were not in Meja at all. You said this was a smaller unit of 20 to 30 men, soldiers. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: It was in Meja, near a tire repair shop. That's where they were, at the edge of the village of Meja.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my question was -- I mean, when he means when he's talking about that, whether he meant that small military unit that assisted him in conversation with Scepanovic, or rather, in this discussion with this Scepanovic. The witness said "yes," but it was not recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, that's noted as a correction to the transcript, Mr. Bakrac. Which paragraph in the statement do we find that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I went off on a tangent and I'm a bit lost in my questions, but if you give me a moment -- it's paragraph 72, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Peraj, is it correct that paramilitaries were different from the Army of Yugoslavia in terms of their hats, ski caps, bandannas, arm-bands, and so on?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it also correct, Mr. Peraj, that you never saw any paramilitary units at the locations where the Army of Yugoslavia was?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I said that there weren't any in the barracks. In the army, normal army barracks, there were no paramilitaries. That's what I said. They weren't even allowed in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Peraj, Mr. Peraj, in paragraph 45, the last sentence, I am going to read it out. You talked about Frenki's men and what they wore. And then you said: "I never saw them at VJ locations."

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: What I mean by "locations" are the barracks, not in the sense of territory. I mean places where there were barracks and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. Peraj, that the Army of Yugoslavia and the MUP in Djakovica had separate commands?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Well, that's normal that the army should have its own command and the police another command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Isn't it only natural, especially in a state of war, that these two commands should have informal meetings between themselves?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes, it's normal; formal and informal meetings. But it's not allowed -- but it's not that it's not allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: At meetings that were held, as you say, twice a day, did you personally ever see General Lazarevic there?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I saw him enter the building there during one of the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You saw him entering the building where the army was stationed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But you did not see him attending meetings.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: It would only be logical, when the commander enters a building where the meeting is being held, it is only logical that he would take part in the meeting, or to observe the meeting, at least, somehow.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But if that is where the command post was, or part of the command, in that building, is it not logical, then, to assume that he went to the command?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Normally meetings were not held in the command. Usually they were held in other places for security reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The building to which you refer was which building? Where you saw Lazarevic enter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the building of the palace of culture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What other things did General Lazarevic normally do at that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what else he did. I think he was visiting the command of the barracks of Gjakova. He was probably giving advice or instructions, commands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honour, for your assistance. We've clarified this now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Peraj, do you know -- I'm sorry. Strike that, please. Mr. Peraj, can you recall when and how many times you saw Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact dates, but I know that it was certainly two times, but I don't remember the exact dates. On one occasion it was the 28th of April, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So on the 28th of April you saw him entering the cultural centre. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: No, no, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm assuming, Mr. Bakrac, that the 28th of April is the event that we've already heard described in the basement of the cafe.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. A few moments ago the witness said that he saw him entering the cultural centre, and I asked him how many times, and he said twice. And I asked about the date, and he said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, that's not what you asked him. You asked him how many times he had seen General Lazarevic. You didn't ask him how many times he had seen him entering the cultural centre. So perhaps you need to clarify the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Where was this basement where you saw him on the 28th of April?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I explained it earlier. It was a building close to Cafe Lajici. The street was called Marsal Tito. Now the street is called Mother Teresa, "Nena Terese."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And what was there in that building?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I did not look around to see what was there in that building. I explained to you about Jeftovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'm asking you what part of the Army of Yugoslavia was there.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: As far as I could see, the temporary headquarters was set up there, of the corps, army corps, and the commander was there, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So in that building the temporary headquarters of the command were located there, only temporarily, right?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Yes, part of the headquarters. Not the whole command, not the entire thing, but part of it was there temporarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What part was that? What part was that that was there?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: Well, I was not the commander to know which parts were there. I saw the people I mentioned earlier. De facto, the commander must have been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So when you say, "the commander must have been there," that means that you never saw him, that you're just assuming this, right?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: No. I said where the commander is the staff must be there. The commander was there. With regard to the other part, I'm not able to say anything about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Peraj, where was the command of the Pristina Corps at that time?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I don't know, sir, where that was, where the command was. The whole -- the entire command, where they were located, I don't know. Because it was logical that the whole building could not contain all of them, all those people, and also because of security reasons they've had to go on the ground and look at things. Sorry, I have to finish this. The command was there, but it was a very small staff. And the security as well, the guards, but I don't know where the entire command was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Peraj, it is your assertion that the command of the Pristina Corps was in Djakovica, not in Pristina. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: No, that's not what I said and that's not what I am saying. Logically, part of the command, with the commander, would be -- was in Gjakova because of the importance of the terrain there, as you stressed yourself, because the forces deployed there between Peja and Decan and Gjakova, Prizren, near the border, there were forces there, so it would be logical --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... explain his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you ought to let him finish his answer, Mr. Bakrac, in view of the uncertainty there is in this matter. Carry on, Mr. Peraj, complete that answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I -- I understand that it would be logical for the commander at that time to be in Gjakova, and he was in Gjakova. It was very important for the deployment in the area, Gjakova-Peja-Decan-Prizren, on that line. We were expecting battles, heavy fighting there. They did not take place, but that's what we were expecting there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Peraj, in line 16 you said that it was logical that he would be there as commander, that is to say that you are basing this on a logical assumption, but it's not that you know this; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ
utterances.text: I know he was. I saw him with my own eyes, I saw him there, in the basement of that building. And it is completely logical for him to be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
